stem: Which measure of center and spread is most appropriate to report for this distribution, and why?
stimulus: A researcher records the time (in minutes) that 40 customers spend in a coffee shop. The distribution of times is strongly right-skewed, with a few customers staying much longer than typical. The five-number summary is: Min = 3, Q1 = 8, Median = 12, Q3 = 18, Max = 65.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean and standard deviation, because they use every data value in the distribution.
choices.rationale: Both the mean and standard deviation are pulled toward the long right tail and the high outlier (65); they are not resistant, so 'uses every value' is not a reason to prefer them for a skewed distribution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean and range, because the range captures the full spread including the long visits.
choices.rationale: The range is determined entirely by the two most extreme values, making it even more sensitive to the outlier than the standard deviation; the mean is also not resistant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Median and IQR, because they are resistant to the strong right skew and the high outlier.
choices.rationale: The median and IQR depend only on the middle portion of the ordered data, so they are not distorted by the skew or the outlier at 65 minutes -- the standard choice for a skewed distribution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Median and standard deviation, because the median is resistant but the shape of the distribution doesn't affect measures of spread.
choices.rationale: This mixes a resistant measure of center with a non-resistant measure of spread; shape and outliers affect standard deviation just as much as they affect the mean.

stem: What is the standard deviation of T?
stimulus: A vending machine dispenses two independent snack items in a bundle. The number of chip bags dispensed has mean 3 and standard deviation 0.8. The number of candy bars dispensed has mean 2 and standard deviation 0.6. Let T = total number of snack items (chips + candy) dispensed in a bundle.

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1.4, because standard deviations of independent random variables add directly.
choices.rationale: Standard deviations do not add directly, even for independent random variables; it is the variances that add.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.2, because the standard deviation of a sum is the difference of the standard deviations.
choices.rationale: This applies the wrong operation entirely; subtracting standard deviations has no statistical justification here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1.96, because the variance of T is the square of the sum of the two standard deviations.
choices.rationale: This squares the sum of the standard deviations (0.8 + 0.6)^2 instead of summing the individual variances, a common algebra-of-variance error.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1.0, because Var(T) = 0.8^2 + 0.6^2 = 0.64 + 0.36 = 1.00, so SD(T) is the square root of 1.00.
choices.rationale: For independent random variables, variances add: Var(T) = Var(chips) + Var(candy) = 0.64 + 0.36 = 1.00, so SD(T) = sqrt(1.00) = 1.0.

stem: Which pair of summary statistics is most appropriate to describe the center and spread?
stimulus: A set of delivery times is strongly right-skewed, with a few very long times.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mean and standard deviation, because they use all the data values.
choices.rationale: Using every value is not an advantage when the distribution is skewed; these measures are not resistant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mean and range, because the range captures the overall spread.
choices.rationale: The range is driven only by the extreme values and is extremely sensitive to outliers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Median and IQR, because they are resistant to the skew and the long right tail.
choices.rationale: Median and IQR are resistant measures, so they are the standard choice for skewed distributions and outliers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Median and standard deviation, because the median is resistant.
choices.rationale: This mixes a resistant center with a non-resistant spread measure.

stem: Which measure is most resistant to the outlier 40?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Range
choices.rationale: The range is entirely determined by the minimum and maximum, so it is not resistant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Standard deviation
choices.rationale: Standard deviation is pulled by extreme values and is not resistant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: IQR
choices.rationale: IQR depends on the middle half of the ordered data and is resistant to a single extreme value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mean
choices.rationale: The mean is also not resistant to outliers.

stem: Which statement is most appropriate?
stimulus: A distribution is roughly symmetric with no outliers.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mean must be much larger than the median.
choices.rationale: That would suggest right skew, not symmetry.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The median must always be larger than the mean.
choices.rationale: There is no such rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mean and median will be close to each other.
choices.rationale: In a roughly symmetric distribution, mean and median tend to be similar.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The range is always the best measure of spread.
choices.rationale: The best measure depends on shape and outliers.

stem: How could blocking help?
stimulus: An experiment compares two diets, but age may affect results.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ignore age because random assignment always eliminates all variation.
choices.rationale: Random assignment reduces confounding but does not remove all variation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Group subjects into age categories before random assignment within each age block.
choices.rationale: Blocking controls a known source of variability by balancing it across treatments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use convenience sampling instead.
choices.rationale: Convenience sampling increases bias and does not block anything.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use the largest age group only.
choices.rationale: This would discard data and does not properly block.

stem: Why is this useful?
stimulus: A medical trial is designed so neither the subjects nor the evaluators know who receives the pill or placebo.

choices.label: A
choices.text: It guarantees the treatment works.
choices.rationale: Blinding does not guarantee effectiveness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It helps reduce placebo effects and observer bias.
choices.rationale: Blinding reduces the chance that expectations affect responses or measurements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It removes the need for random assignment.
choices.rationale: Random assignment is still needed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It makes the sample larger.
choices.rationale: Blinding does not change sample size.

stem: What is the probability of success on both stages?
stimulus: A two-stage process has P(first success) = 0.3 and P(second success | first success) = 0.5.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This adds probabilities instead of multiplying along the path.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Multiply along the path: 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Multiplies 0.7 (the probability the first stage does not succeed) by 0.5 instead of 0.3 by 0.5: 0.7 × 0.5 = 0.35.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Treats the two probabilities as overlapping events and adds them, 0.3 + 0.5 − 0.15 = 0.65, instead of multiplying 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15 for both stages succeeding.

stem: What features are needed for a binomial setting?
stimulus: A basketball player makes a free throw with probability 0.7 on each attempt.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any random experiment with numerical outcomes.
choices.rationale: Not every random experiment is binomial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fixed number of trials, independent trials, two outcomes per trial, and a constant success probability.
choices.rationale: Those are the standard binomial conditions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least three outcomes on each trial.
choices.rationale: Binomial trials have only two outcomes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A changing success probability from trial to trial.
choices.rationale: Constant p is required.

topic: 4.2 (registered; content is a proportion CI, so 3.3)
stem: What happens if the sample size increases and all else stays the same?
stimulus: A 95% confidence interval for a population proportion has margin of error 0.04.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The margin of error gets larger.
choices.rationale: That is the opposite of the sample-size effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The margin of error stays exactly the same.
choices.rationale: Sample size affects SE and MOE.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The margin of error gets smaller.
choices.rationale: Larger samples reduce standard error, which shrinks the margin of error.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The margin of error becomes negative.
choices.rationale: Margins of error are never negative.

stem: What is the power of the test?
stimulus: A study has β = 0.25 for a particular test.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: That is β, the Type II error rate.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Power = 1 - β = 0.75.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: That would be α in many settings, not power.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is not 1 - β here.

stem: Which formula correctly finds P(machine B | defective)?
stimulus: A factory has three machines with different defect rates and production shares.

choices.label: A
choices.text: P(B)P(defective)
choices.rationale: This is not conditional probability; it omits the denominator.

choices.label: B
choices.text: P(B | defective) = P(B) / P(defective | B)
choices.rationale: That is not Bayes’ theorem.

choices.label: C
choices.text: P(defective | B) + P(B)
choices.rationale: Probabilities are not combined this way.

choices.label: D
choices.text: P(defective | B)P(B) / P(defective)
choices.rationale: Bayes’ theorem reverses the conditional probability using the defect probability in the numerator and the total defect probability in the denominator.

stem: What is the mean?
stimulus: A random variable takes values 1, 2, and 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, and 0.3.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This likely comes from a rough average rather than the weighted mean.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is not the correct weighted average.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is the largest outcome, not the mean.

stem: Which student performed better relative to their own test's distribution, and by how many standard deviations above the mean?
stimulus: On a nationally normed exam, scores are approximately normally distributed with mean 500 and standard deviation 100. Fatima scores 640. On a different, unrelated diagnostic test with mean 20 and standard deviation 4, Diego scores 26.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diego, because his z-score of 1.5 is higher than Fatima's z-score of 1.4.
choices.rationale: Fatima's z-score is (640 - 500)/100 = 1.4. Diego's z-score is (26 - 20)/4 = 1.5. Standardizing puts both scores on the same scale, and Diego's is higher.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fatima, because 640 is a higher raw score than 26.
choices.rationale: Comparing raw scores directly ignores that the two tests have completely different means and standard deviations; raw scores from different distributions are not comparable without standardizing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fatima, because her raw score is farther from her test's mean (140 points) than Diego's is from his (6 points).
choices.rationale: Comparing raw point distances from the mean ignores the different scales (standard deviations) of the two tests; 140 points on a test with SD 100 is less extreme than 6 points on a test with SD 4.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two students performed identically, because both scored above their test's mean.
choices.rationale: Both scoring above the mean does not mean the performances are equivalent; the magnitude of each score's standardized distance from the mean still needs to be compared.

stem: As the sample size n increases from 10 to 100, what happens to the shape and variability of the sampling distribution of x-bar?
stimulus: Strongly right-skewed household incomes in a large city; random sample of n households, sample mean x-bar.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The shape becomes more skewed and the variability increases, matching the population more closely as n grows.
choices.rationale: This reverses both effects of the Central Limit Theorem; larger samples make the sampling distribution of the mean look less like the skewed population, not more.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The shape stays exactly as skewed as the population, but the variability decreases.
choices.rationale: This ignores the Central Limit Theorem's effect on shape; as n increases, the sampling distribution of x-bar becomes more normal, not equally skewed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The shape becomes more normal and the variability (standard error) decreases.
choices.rationale: The Central Limit Theorem states that as n increases, the sampling distribution of x-bar becomes more approximately normal regardless of population shape, and its standard error (population SD divided by the square root of n) decreases as n increases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The shape becomes more normal, but the variability stays the same regardless of n.
choices.rationale: This correctly describes the shape change but incorrectly claims the standard error is unaffected by sample size, when in fact it decreases as n increases.

stem: What is the z-score for a student who scored 78?
stimulus: A test has mean 70 and standard deviation 8.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This subtracts the mean but does not standardize by the standard deviation.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This divides by 10 instead of 8 or treats the difference incorrectly.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The sign is wrong; 78 is above the mean.

stem: Which statement about the median is correct?
stimulus: A data set has 20 observations ordered from least to greatest.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The median is the 10th value only.
choices.rationale: That would be true only for an odd number of observations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The median is the average of the 10th and 11th values.
choices.rationale: For an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The median is the difference between the 10th and 11th values.
choices.rationale: Median is an average, not a difference.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The median is the mean of all 20 values.
choices.rationale: That describes the mean, not the median.

stem: What is the best method?
stimulus: A teacher wants a random sample of 30 students from a list of 300.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Choose the first 30 students in alphabetical order.
choices.rationale: This is not random and may be biased.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Choose only students who volunteer.
choices.rationale: Volunteers create voluntary-response bias.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Assign each student a number and use a random number generator to select 30 numbers.
choices.rationale: A simple random sample gives every student an equal chance of being selected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Choose every student whose birthday is in January.
choices.rationale: This is systematic by a nonrandom rule and may be biased.

stem: Which is a plausible confounding variable?
stimulus: A study finds that students who sleep more also score higher on tests.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The regression slope
choices.rationale: The slope is part of the analysis, not a lurking variable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sample size
choices.rationale: Sample size affects precision, not the causal mechanism in the same way.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Study habits or prior preparation
choices.rationale: A third variable could affect both sleep and test scores, producing the observed association.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The p-value
choices.rationale: The p-value is a summary of evidence, not a confounder.

stem: What is this called?
stimulus: A principal asks every student in the school to fill out a survey.

choices.label: A
choices.text: A random sample
choices.rationale: A random sample selects only some members of the population by chance. Here every student is asked, so nothing is sampled and the survey is a census.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A stratified sample
choices.rationale: There is no subsampling by strata here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A census
choices.rationale: A census collects data from every member of the population of interest.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A biased sample
choices.rationale: A census may still have nonresponse issues, but it is still a census by definition.

stem: What is the expected value?
stimulus: A game pays $10 with probability 0.2 and $0 otherwise.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is the prize amount, not the expected value.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This is 10 x 0.8, which uses the wrong probability.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: There is a positive probability of winning, so the expected value is not zero.

stem: Which counting method is appropriate?
stimulus: A club wants to choose 3 officers from 10 members, with no order.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Permutation
choices.rationale: Permutation counts ordered arrangements, which is not needed here.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Multiplication rule only
choices.rationale: That alone does not account for choosing without order.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Combination
choices.rationale: When order does not matter, use combinations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Binomial distribution
choices.rationale: This is a counting situation, not a binomial probability setting.

stem: Which sample has the smaller standard error?
stimulus: Two samples are taken from the same population, one with n = 25 and one with n = 100.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sample with n = 25.
choices.rationale: Smaller samples have larger standard error.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sample with n = 100.
choices.rationale: SE decreases as n increases because the denominator sqrt(n) gets larger.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both samples have the same SE.
choices.rationale: Sample size changes the SE.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither sample has an SE.
choices.rationale: Every sample mean has a standard error in this context.

stem: What should the statistical decision be?
stimulus: A test gives p-value = 0.018 and alpha = 0.05.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fail to reject H0 because the p-value is not zero.
choices.rationale: A p-value does not need to be zero to reject the null.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accept H0 as proven true.
choices.rationale: We do not prove the null hypothesis true.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ignore the p-value and use the sample mean only.
choices.rationale: Inference is based on the p-value and significance level.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reject H0; the result is statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
choices.rationale: Since p < alpha, the evidence is strong enough to reject the null hypothesis.

stem: What is the expected count in the cell?
stimulus: A chi-square table cell has row total 40, column total 50, and grand total 200.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This adds the row and column totals instead of using the expected-count formula: 40 + 50 = 90.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses half the grand total as the denominator: (40x50)/100 = 20.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Expected count = (row total x column total) / grand total = 40x50/200 = 10.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This uses double the grand total as the denominator: (40x50)/400 = 5.

stem: What type of error occurred?
stimulus: A null hypothesis is rejected even though it is actually true.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type II error
choices.rationale: Type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type I error
choices.rationale: A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sampling error
choices.rationale: This is a more general term, not the specific hypothesis-test error.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No error
choices.rationale: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is an error.

stem: Which conclusion is appropriately supported by this study design?
stimulus: A wellness magazine reports that people who meditate at least 20 minutes per day have lower blood pressure on average than people who do not meditate, based on a survey of 500 adults who volunteered to report their meditation habits and blood pressure.

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is an association between meditation habits and blood pressure in this sample, but causation cannot be concluded because participants were not randomly assigned to meditate or not.
choices.rationale: This was an observational, voluntary-response study with no random assignment of the explanatory variable, so an association can be described but a causal claim is not supported.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Meditating for 20 minutes a day causes lower blood pressure.
choices.rationale: This draws a causal conclusion from an observational study with no random assignment, which cannot rule out confounding variables.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the sample size is large (500 people), causation can be concluded even without random assignment.
choices.rationale: A large sample size reduces sampling variability but does nothing to address confounding; only random assignment supports causal claims.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No conclusion can be drawn because the study did not use a randomized experiment.
choices.rationale: This overcorrects -- observational studies can still support conclusions about association, just not causation.

stem: Why is it inappropriate to use a normal approximation for the sampling distribution of p-hat in this situation?
stimulus: A quality control engineer wants to use a normal approximation for the sampling distribution of the sample proportion of defective items in a random sample of size n = 40 from a manufacturing process where the true defect rate is p = 0.03.

choices.label: A
choices.text: np = 40(0.03) = 1.2, which is less than 10, so the success-failure condition is not met and the sampling distribution of p-hat would be skewed, not approximately normal.
choices.rationale: The success-failure condition requires both np and n(1-p) to be at least 10 (a common threshold); here np = 1.2, which fails the condition, so the normal approximation is not justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sample size 40 is too small to ever use a normal approximation, regardless of p.
choices.rationale: Appropriateness depends on np and n(1-p), not on the sample size n alone; a sample of 40 could be adequate for a different value of p.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The population defect rate p = 0.03 is a parameter, not a statistic, so the normal approximation does not apply to parameters.
choices.rationale: This confuses the parameter/statistic distinction with the actual condition being checked; the success-failure condition uses p to check np and n(1-p), regardless of p being a parameter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Random sampling was not used, so no approximation is valid.
choices.rationale: The stimulus states the sample is random; this introduces an assumption violation that isn't actually present in the scenario.

stem: How does the mean change?
stimulus: A data set has 12 values with mean 40. One value is changed from 18 to 30.

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases by 12.
choices.rationale: That is the change in one data value, not the change in the mean.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It does not change.
choices.rationale: Changing a data value changes the mean unless the change is zero.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases by 0.5.
choices.rationale: This divides by the wrong number of values.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It increases by 1.0, because the total sum increases by 12 and the data set has 12 values.
choices.rationale: Changing one value by +12 raises the mean by 12/12 = 1.

stem: What is the upper fence for possible outliers?
stimulus: For a data set, Q1 = 18 and Q3 = 30.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses 1.0(IQR) instead of 1.5(IQR).

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This mistakenly starts from Q1 instead of Q3: Q1 + 1.5(IQR) = 18 + 1.5(12) = 18 + 18 = 36.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This doubles Q3 instead of adding 1.5×IQR to it: 2 × Q3 = 2(30) = 60.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: IQR = 12, so the upper fence is Q3 + 1.5(IQR) = 30 + 18 = 48.

stem: Why might stratified sampling be better than a simple random sample?
stimulus: A school has freshmen, sophomores, juniors, and seniors in different proportions.

choices.label: A
choices.text: It ensures each grade level is represented in the sample.
choices.rationale: Stratified sampling can improve representativeness when important subgroups need guaranteed representation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It guarantees no bias under any circumstance.
choices.rationale: No sampling method guarantees zero bias.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It always requires fewer people than any other method.
choices.rationale: Sample size depends on the precision desired, not just the method.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It removes the need for random selection.
choices.rationale: Strata are typically sampled randomly within each group.

stem: What does random assignment help with most?
stimulus: A school randomly assigns students to a new tutoring program or the old program.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Guaranteeing a perfectly equal sample size in every subgroup.
choices.rationale: Random assignment does not guarantee equal subgroup sizes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eliminating all measurement error.
choices.rationale: Random assignment does not fix measurement problems.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Making the study automatically double blind.
choices.rationale: Blinding is separate from random assignment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Balancing lurking variables between the groups so a causal comparison is more credible.
choices.rationale: Random assignment helps create comparable groups and supports causal inference.

stem: What is P(honor roll | athlete)?
stimulus: In a class of 40 students, 10 are athletes, and 4 of those athletes are on the honor roll.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Conditional probability uses the athlete group as the denominator.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses the whole class instead of only the athletes.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is P(athlete), not the conditional probability.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This incorrectly uses the number of athletes NOT on the honor roll (10 − 4 = 6) as the denominator instead of all 10 athletes: 4/6 ≈ 0.67.

stem: What is the probability that it does not rain?
stimulus: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 0.25.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Use the complement: 1 - 0.25 = 0.75.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This repeats the original probability instead of its complement.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is not the complement of 0.25.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This does not sum with 0.25 to 1.

stem: What is P(A or B)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Use the addition rule: P(A or B) = 0.6 + 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.9.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This subtracts too much or omits one event.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This adds the probabilities without correcting for overlap.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is only the intersection.

stem: What is the main problem?
stimulus: A new estimator consistently misses the true value by a large amount, even with large samples.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only variability
choices.rationale: Large random scatter is not the only issue when the estimator is consistently off target.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normality
choices.rationale: Normality is not the central issue described here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Independence
choices.rationale: The question is about systematic error, not dependence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bias
choices.rationale: If an estimator is systematically off target, the estimator is biased.

stem: Which hypotheses are correct?
stimulus: A survey of 200 people finds 118 support a policy. The question is whether support exceeds 50%.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Null and alternative are reversed.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: The claim is that support exceeds 50%, so this is a right-tailed test for a proportion.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses the wrong parameter symbol.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Proportions are not counts.

stem: What is P(X = 0)?
stimulus: A binomial setting has n = 5 and p = 0.5.

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: That is the probability of a single success, not zero successes in five trials.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is not the correct binomial calculation for zero successes.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: That is the trial count, not a probability.

stem: Which study is most likely to have lower power?
stimulus: Two studies test the same claim, but one uses a more stringent significance level and a smaller sample size.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The study with the smaller sample size and more stringent α.
choices.rationale: Lower α and smaller n both tend to reduce power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The study with the larger sample size and more stringent α.
choices.rationale: Larger n increases power, all else equal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The study with the larger sample size and larger α.
choices.rationale: Larger α increases power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both studies must have the same power.
choices.rationale: Power depends on n and α, so they need not match.

stem: What is the primary statistical benefit of this design compared to completely randomizing fertilizer type across all 40 plants without regard to sun exposure?
stimulus: A researcher wants to test whether a new fertilizer increases tomato plant yield compared to a standard fertilizer. She has 40 tomato plants: 20 grown in full-sun plots and 20 grown in partial-shade plots. She plans to randomly assign fertilizer type (new vs. standard) separately within the full-sun group and separately within the partial-shade group, rather than randomizing across all 40 plants at once.

choices.label: A
choices.text: It removes the need for random assignment altogether, since sun exposure is already controlled.
choices.rationale: Blocking does not replace random assignment; fertilizer type is still randomly assigned within each sun-exposure block.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It guarantees that the new fertilizer will outperform the standard fertilizer within each sun-exposure group.
choices.rationale: Blocking controls a source of variability; it does not guarantee any particular outcome for either treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reduces variability in yield due to sun exposure, making it easier to detect a true difference between fertilizers if one exists.
choices.rationale: Blocking by a known nuisance variable (sun exposure) removes its variability from the comparison between fertilizers, increasing the power to detect a real treatment effect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It increases the sample size available for comparing the fertilizers.
choices.rationale: Blocking reorganizes how the same 40 plants are grouped and randomized; it does not add any additional plants or observations.

stem: Which is a correct interpretation of this confidence interval?
stimulus: A polling organization constructs a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of adults in a state who support a new transportation initiative and obtains the interval (0.46, 0.54) based on a random sample of 800 adults.

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is a 95% probability that the true population proportion is between 0.46 and 0.54.
choices.rationale: The true population proportion is a fixed (though unknown) number, not a random variable, so it is incorrect to assign a probability to it falling in a specific interval.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 95% of adults in the state support the initiative, plus or minus 4 percentage points.
choices.rationale: This confuses the confidence interval for the unknown population proportion with a statement about what fraction of individual adults support the initiative.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If this exact sample were surveyed 100 times, the sample proportion would fall between 0.46 and 0.54 ninety-five times.
choices.rationale: "95% confidence" describes the long-run behavior of the method across many different random samples, not repeated surveys of the same fixed sample.

choices.label: D
choices.text: We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.46 to 0.54 captures the true proportion of all adults in the state who support the initiative, based on the method used to construct it.
choices.rationale: This correctly ties the 95% confidence level to the reliability of the interval-construction method over repeated random sampling, rather than to a probability statement about the fixed parameter.

stem: Which description best matches the distribution?
stimulus: A boxplot has a long right whisker and one high outlier.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Right-skewed with a high outlier.
choices.rationale: A long right whisker and a high outlier indicate right skew.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Left-skewed with a low outlier.
choices.rationale: This describes the opposite tail behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Approximately symmetric with no outliers.
choices.rationale: The long right tail and outlier contradict symmetry.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bimodal with two clusters.
choices.rationale: A boxplot does not by itself show two modes, and nothing here indicates bimodality.

stem: What does that mean?
stimulus: A score is at the 75th percentile on a test.

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 75% of scores are at or below that score.
choices.rationale: Percentiles describe the percentage of observations at or below the given value.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The score is 75 points higher than the mean.
choices.rationale: Percentile does not measure distance from the mean.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 75% of scores are above that score.
choices.rationale: That would describe the 25th percentile, not the 75th.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The score is the average of the top 75% of scores.
choices.rationale: That is not what a percentile means.

stem: What type of study is this?
stimulus: Researchers record whether students study music and whether they prefer online lectures. They do not assign any treatment.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Randomized experiment
choices.rationale: No random assignment or imposed treatment is described.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Case-control experiment
choices.rationale: This is not an experimental design.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Double-blind trial
choices.rationale: No treatment or blinding is described.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Observational study
choices.rationale: The researchers only observe existing behavior and do not impose a treatment.

stem: What bias is most likely?
stimulus: A survey is conducted only by texting students with smartphones.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Undercoverage bias
choices.rationale: Students without smartphones are systematically left out of the sample frame.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Response bias only
choices.rationale: The main issue is that some students are excluded before response occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No bias because texting is random.
choices.rationale: The sample frame is not representative of all students.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Placebo effect
choices.rationale: Placebo effects apply to experiments, not surveys.

stem: Are A and B independent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, because P(A) and P(B) are not equal.
choices.rationale: Equal probabilities are not required for independence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, because the events both have probabilities less than 1.
choices.rationale: Having probabilities less than 1 does not decide independence. Independence is checked by comparing P(A and B) with P(A)P(B): here 0.3 x 0.4 = 0.12, which equals P(A and B), so A and B are independent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because A and B cannot both happen.
choices.rationale: That would describe mutually exclusive events, not independence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, because P(A)P(B) = 0.12 = P(A and B).
choices.rationale: Independence holds when the joint probability equals the product of the marginal probabilities.

stem: Can the card be both a heart and a spade?
stimulus: A single card is drawn from a standard deck.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes, because all suits overlap.
choices.rationale: Suits are distinct categories.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, if the card is red.
choices.rationale: Red does not make a card both a heart and a spade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No, because the events are independent.
choices.rationale: Mutually exclusive is the relevant idea, not independence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No, because those events are mutually exclusive.
choices.rationale: One card cannot belong to two different suits at the same time.

stem: Why is the sampling distribution of x-bar often approximately normal?
stimulus: A population is strongly skewed, but n = 50 random samples are taken.

choices.label: A
choices.text: By the Central Limit Theorem, large samples tend to produce an approximately normal sampling distribution of x-bar.
choices.rationale: The CLT says the sampling distribution of the mean becomes approximately normal as n grows large.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because every population is normal when n = 50.
choices.rationale: The population itself does not become normal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the sample mean always equals the population mean.
choices.rationale: The sample mean varies from sample to sample.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because skewness disappears in the raw data.
choices.rationale: The raw data can still be skewed.

stem: What is the standard error of p-hat?
stimulus: A sample proportion uses p-hat with p = 0.4 and n = 100.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: numerator p(1-p), not SE

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: the proportion

stem: Which study is more likely to have greater power, all else equal?
stimulus: Two studies test the same hypothesis, but one has a much larger sample size.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The study with the smaller sample size.
choices.rationale: Smaller samples usually have less power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The study with the larger sample size.
choices.rationale: Larger samples reduce SE and usually make it easier to detect a true effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They must have the same power.
choices.rationale: Sample size affects power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Power depends only on the p-value.
choices.rationale: Power is about the test design and true effect, not the observed p-value alone.

stem: Which conclusion is correct?
stimulus: A test reports p = 0.12 and alpha = 0.05.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reject H0 because p is less than 1.
choices.rationale: The p-value is compared with alpha, not with 1. Here p = 0.12 > 0.05, so not enough evidence to reject H0.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accept H0 as proven.
choices.rationale: We do not prove the null true.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fail to reject H0; the result is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
choices.rationale: Because p > alpha, the evidence is not strong enough to reject the null.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The alternative hypothesis is true with probability 0.12.
choices.rationale: That is a common misinterpretation of p-values.
